utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello, Your Honours. It's IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. We are the 2nd of October, and a Monday today. I'd like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, the attorneys for the Prosecution, the witness, the Defence counsel representing the accused, as well as the accused who are sitting at the back of the courtroom. I should also like to greet all the people who are giving us a helping hand. As you have realised we have switched courtrooms. We are now in courtroom number I and not courtroom number III. This is a slightly different courtroom because we sit closer to the Defence counsel and the Prosecution attorneys, but the accused sit much further away from us than they do in courtroom number III. I don't know whether I told you already, but this week we were due to sit on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, we were supposed to be sitting in the afternoon, but as this courtroom is empty, we shall have our hearing tomorrow morning, Wednesday morning and Thursday morning in this courtroom. So make your arrangements to fit this new schedule. The hearings will be held in the morning. I would also like to point out to you the fact that the witness list has been disclosed to us last week. We've already mentioned it. There is a witness which we shall be hearing for a period of two days, and then we have another three witnesses who will be testifying pursuant to Rule 89(F). In addition, Judge Mindua is not here today and will not be able to attend throughout the week. Pursuant to Rule 15 bis, he shall not attend the hearing throughout the week. If there are no urgent matters to be discussed, we shall hear the witness and hear the swearing in of the -- the swearing of the witness. The Prosecution had intended the examination-in-chief to last three hours, which means that the Defence will have three and a half hours and Mr. Praljak should have at least one hour, given that Mr. Praljak has met the witness. Mr. Praljak should have at least one hour, unless the other accused give him some of their time. So, Witness, could you please stand up. You shall spell out your first name and family name and give me your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Peter Hauenstein, born 29th of January, 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me what your current occupation is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a military officer in the Canadian Forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me in 1992 and 1993, where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where was I; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1993, I was seconded from the Canadian Forces into the ECMM mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified before an International Tribunal about the events that unfolded in the former republics of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me in what case you have already testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember that at this time. That was about a year and half ago, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't remember, but I do remember, because you testified in Hadzihasanovic and I was the Presiding Judge. And in the 800-page judgement -- now, on pages 3603, 3720, 3739 your name has been mentioned three times in the judgement that was rendered in that case. Please read the text of the solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we start this hearing, I would just like to explain a few things to you. As you know, this is a common law procedure. To begin with, you will have to answer a number of questions which will be put to you by the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor whom you have met, undoubtedly, during the proofing session. The Prosecutor, as I had mentioned a few minutes ago, had planned for three hours of examination-in-chief. When the questions will be put to you, the Prosecutor will certainly show you a number of documents which you probably have before you. If you don't have them before you, maybe it would be easier that you were provided with a set of documents so that you can go straight to the document which is being mentioned. There are tabs for each document so you can find your way around easily. At the end of the examination-in-chief, there are six Defence counsel on the other side who will be taking the floor, and these Defence counsel will put you questions, and this will be part of the cross-examination. The cross-examination is designed to test your credibility, and the Defence counsel will put questions to you and some of the questions come from the accused whom they represent here. The Trial Chamber wishes to respect due process and wishes to be transparent in this case, and the accused are entitled to put you -- questions to you directly. So if the accused feel it is necessary, they will put questions to you. There are three Judges that form the Bench. Generally speaking, there are four Judges. Today we are three. And the Judges, when they feel it is necessary, can always put questions to you. As a rule, we sometimes want a clarification -- a clarification point concerning an answer you have provided or because we feel we want to try to understand what the truth in the matter is. Sometimes an eyewitness can help the Bench when the Bench has to rule on the relevance and probative value of evidence material. This is why we have become accustomed to intervene and put questions directly to the witness sometimes. Please try and be as concise and accurate as you can, because vague answers are not really useful to the person putting the question and is even less useful to justice in general. But I have -- I'm not much concerned about that. If you feel that a question has not been put to you properly, please ask the person to reformulate the question so you understand, as you should. If you have a problem, do not hesitate to let us know about it. As you know, because you have already testified before this Tribunal, every hour and a half we make a technical break, a 20-minute break, which means that the hearing will conclude at 7.00 this evening, and we shall resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 until a quarter to 2.00. So you will be able to get back home tomorrow afternoon if there is a flight available. Let me now turn to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to ask a short question. What is your grade in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Colonel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you rather be called colonel or sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel is fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My name is Vassily Poryvaev; I am counsel for the Prosecution. I have a number of questions to Witness Haunstein. Colonel, to what position in Bosnia-Herzegovina ECMM mission you were appointed?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: In 1993, I was seconded from the Canadian military into the OSCE and down into the ECMM as an ECMM monitor for a period of about seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: To what team were you appointed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. Just a short question I would like to put to you. Canada is not part of the EU, so as a Canadian, in what capacity were you there? I would like to repeat because my microphone was cut off. You are a Canadian citizen and you were part of a European mission. As far as I know, Canada is not part of the EU. So in what capacity were you, as a Canadian, enrolled in an EU mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During that time frame there had been an agreement between the Canadian government, and as a member of the OSCE, there was assistance required from the European Community in those days that asked that Canada participate in the mission by providing observers. In any given six-, seven-month rotation, 12 observers were given from Canada, all from the military, and moved through the OSCE and into the ECMM as the monitors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So I repeat my question. To what position were you appointed in 1993, in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: In Bosnia I was placed in a team, Victor 2, which was located in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What are the areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were included in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: My area of responsibility covered three major communities: Bugojno in the north, Gornji Vakuf in the centre, and Prozor to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that the abbreviated name of your team was V2?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct, Victor 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Colonel, I suggest that before going down to mission you had a sort of training, whether in Canada or in Zagreb. Did you have it?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We were initially warned off. I at the time happened to be serving as a squadron commander in my regiment, and from that point, once identified, then I moved to Ottawa for a period of time where I underwent training and cultural awareness, which also included mission awareness. From there, once the mission was given a go, we were moved from Ottawa into Zagreb and met up with the EC Monitoring Mission headquarters, and in that location we underwent further training for about a week, familiarisation training and, once again, mission-specific training, and then we were deployed to our areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday, we agreed upon that you speak a little bit slower, not only for the people present here in the courtroom but for the interpreters as well.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have any special training on a system of communication that would be in use in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: There were three forms of communication that were provided to us. One was cell telephones, the next was HF radio, and the third was a system called Capsat, which was a computer-based programme which used to communicate with a satellite and was used to communicate around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Were all entities of ECMM mission to Bosnia equipped with Capsat system?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: As I was aware, yes. Each team had a Capsat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: How did you communicate with UNPROFOR or humanitarian organisations? By what method of communication? Did they also have Capsat system?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: No, they did not. In my specific Victor 2, we enjoyed a unique relationship with UNPROFOR in that, in those days, within Gornji Vakuf there was a British company assigned to UNPROFOR, at which point in time we shared, or I managed to acquire from their stocks, a military radio which I also had installed in my vehicle and was able to stay in constant contact with them. As for NGOs and humanitarian organisations, it was a matter of meeting them on the ground face to face. But there was no formal communication other than the connection with UNPROFOR or UNHCR convoys which may be coming in, and we got it via UNPROFOR that these convoys would be moving in our direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Colonel, what was your understanding of your functions as a member of ECMM mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: The function is summed up in the name of the mission, the European Community Monitoring Mission. We were there to monitor the activities that were ongoing in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time in 1993. A lot of that was specifically not just realising the military situation but also the humanitarian situation, which had deteriorated within that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Were you supposed to coordinate your actions with humanitarian organisations, UNPROFOR, other organisations which were involved in issues in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: It was my understanding that it was a given that our relationship was as -- I'll start from the beginning. It was felt that we took on a specific mission to be the glue between the organisations that were on the ground. There was a close relationship, yes, with UNPROFOR, but also we developed relationships with many NGOs and humanitarian organisations that were at work. We tended to become the eyes and the ears on the ground in a very unfortunate situation in which a lot of the humanitarian organisations and NGOs were in our area only on occasion. And consequently we ended up being the wherewithal for them to understand the situation when they came into our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Colonel, since you yourself just told us that you were the eyes and the ears on the ground, where did you take your information?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: It was from a variety of resources, including those immediately next to us. And what I'm referring to is our relationship with UNPROFOR, who, of course, had a whole company in that area, and there was a close relationship developed between that company and my team, as well as many, like I said, NGOs that worked - ICRC, UNHCR, and Medecins sans Frontieres and such organisations such as that. As well, on the ground we developed relationships with the Bosniaks on one side and, of course, the Croats on the other side, all the way down the chain of command within the military as well as civilians, in the structure of mayors and councillors within each of those areas; and last but not least, a relationship with the religious organisations on both sides which included the Catholic church on one side and the Muslim on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity of having close relations with laymen?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely. In some cases we ended up interacting with individuals on the ground. In those days it was a very difficult situation in which to manoeuvre, but, you know, we came upon soldiers, civilians alike on the ground and were able to talk with them through my interpreter and gather information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: How many people were there in your team? And what was your official, let's say, title?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: In those days I would say my official title was the team leader. The team consisted, and it varied depending on what was happening, but for all intents and purposes, it was two observers and one driver. So it was myself, my partner and a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your partner, was he, in fact or de jure, your deputy?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes. For all intents and purposes that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: There were two individuals in the time that I was in there. One was Skat-Rordam, which was a Danish --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Don't hurry, please. Spell his name.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Oh, boy. S-k-a-t, R-o-r-d-a-m, I believe, if I remember correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And the second one?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: And the second one was Rudy, and I'm sorry, I cannot at this time remember his last name. His first name is spelled R-u-d-y.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe in the course of our examination-in-chief you will recall his name, and then remind us that you just -- his name, just to get to your mind. General, now let's move to the structure of the ECMM organisations on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and in particular on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let's start with upper echelons. What was the highest body of ECMM on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, at the time when you were on mission?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: As I recall, the ECMM headquarters was located in Zagreb, and from there, there was a structure, which was located throughout the area of conflict, which also included teams to the east in Bulgaria, Macedonia, and then, of course, into Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now, in --

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: And Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: The structure in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: And the structure in Bosnia-Herzegovina was, as I understood, there was an RC, which stood for regional centre, in Zenica. Underneath the regional centre in Zenica were a CC in Travnik, and then under CC Travnik was my team, Victor 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please explain to the Trial Chamber what stands for "CC".

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Coordination centre, if I remember correctly, is what it stood for. So you had a coordination centre, a regional centre, and then the major headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what was -- who was your immediate commander? Was that commander within coordination centre or regional centre?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I think the -- first, we have to understand the word "commander." I don't think we used the word "commander." We were not in military uniforms. I would say my next higher supervisor resided in CC Travnik, and his name was Philip Watkins in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who was your superior in Zenica regional centre?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: The regional centre was a French diplomat by the name of Pierre Thebault, if I remember correctly. It was a hyphenated name, I think. Once again I'd have to refer to the reports of the day which has his name at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we'll pass on to the system of reporting within ECM mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So you were the lowest, let's say, unity within this mission and you were on the ground.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please explain to the Trial Chamber the system of your reporting.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: We were asked to produce a daily report, approximately, if I remember correctly, between 1800 and 2000 hours each evening, of which was submitted to our next higher headquarters, i.e., CC Travnik; but at the same time we had to carbon copy our reports to our parallel or flanking organisations and our higher organisations. So at the same time, RC Zenica and Zagreb would also receive our daily report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you submit your daily report also to ECMM liaison officer in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That liaison officer was an ECM representative at UNPROFOR headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Colonel, were there any other regional centres or coordination centres of ECMM on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, in particular in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the adjacent areas?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I can remember -- you know, once again, I would have to refer to daily reports. But there was one in Mostar; the other one was in Tuzla; Zenica, which I've already mentioned; Travnik I mentioned; and I believe there was one even down to the south-west in Tomislavgrad. I'm at a blank right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you communicate with them on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely. It was our lifeline.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of communication was it?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Once again, it was that daily report via Capsat that we communicated with each other, as well as, on occasion, when we could get it, we used HF and as well as cell telephone when the network was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Where did you have your headquarters, I mean team V2?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Victor 2 was collocated with the UNPROFOR company in Gornji Vakuf, in the warehouse outside of the small town of Gornji Vakuf, to the immediate east, about 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When you say collocating, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Our office and the living quarters were in the same building as UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: In the same building or in the same space even?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct. Our office -- my office specifically was in the same office as the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: UNPROFOR office from what country?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: It was from the UK, and it was from the Prince of Wales Regiment, of which A company, which was in fact B Company, that company which was B Company, that resided and was there in that area and had their area of responsibility very similar to ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who commanded that company?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: At that time, Major Graham Binns, spelled B-i-n-n-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity of sharing information with them once you were sitting in the same office?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Once again, it was essential that we shared information because of his capability of a full company, including a formal military structure, which included platoons with platoon leaders and of course vehicles. I was one team and had one vehicle. So absolutely, we shared information. And because of the unique relationship I enjoyed with the company commander, we represented ourselves equally at given meetings, and at times we had to split and share information based on the fact that he was in one location and I was in another and, in some cases, enjoyed more freedom of movement than UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you at some point plan, let's say, joint operations?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes. On many different occasions we did, either by having joint meetings or, in fact, doing and visiting areas jointly. Once again, his vehicles were -- and especially in the very -- more dangerous areas, I, in fact, travelled in UNPROFOR vehicles because they were armoured.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now let's pass on to just dissemination on information from the, let's say, highest echelons of ECMM to the ground units. What kind of documents, information, did you receive from the Zagreb headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: The biggest understanding is the fact that there was a given method of dissemination of information which was to ensure that everybody knew what was going on around them, below them, and above them. Now, our report was only one of many reports that were disseminated or received, understanding, in a normal structure, at the lowest level which was residing, I was responsible for initiating the initial report on the ground, which then, throughout the evening, would be rolled up into the CC Travnik daily report, which would then, in turn, be wrapped up into the RC Zenica report, and then from the RC Zenica would go up to, of course, Zagreb, to the headquarters. And all along the way, your information was rolled up and was, in fact, disseminated back to you, and so you had a good understanding what was happening to your left and right flank as well as up -- once again, up and down the chain. There was also information that was wrapped up specifically on specific issues. The standard report that we used kind of divided information into military aspects, political, humanitarian, and a general summary of what had occurred. As --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: As an example, the humanitarian side of the house, there was actually humanitarian structure at the headquarters in Zagreb which would pull in all information from across the whole area and wrap up in a weekly humanitarian report back down to us across the whole structure. So you got kind of a week's summary in what had transpired in the humanitarian aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you receive any compilation of information from regional centres or coordination centres?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely, on a daily basis. Once again, our report was done once every day, which was due at a certain time. I said I think it was either 1800 or 2000 hours. And then from there, by midnight we would be starting to receive the wrapped up culmination of the CC Travnik report, then the RC Zenica report, which would be -- which we would, of course, receive on Capsat and read that report and understand it and how it affected us in our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any feedback from ECMM liaison officer in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes. We had received -- part of the reporting setup was also inclusive of the ECLO because they, of course, had a direct link at the UNPROFOR headquarters location and it just kind of culminated and enabled that information we were sharing was, in fact, getting through. I use the example, once again, that we shared information -- I shared information with the company commander, and it was very comforting to see that the information that would come back down his chain and the information that would come back down my chain would easily fit one into the other, because of the -- it was the same information that was going up both chains.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Colonel, when you received such kind of information or compilation reports from your upper, just, bodies, did you ever notice that the information had been edited, amended, or alterated [sic] [Realtime transcript read in error "alterated in any way"]?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I think the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I object to the question. I think we need to have some background information, at least a predicate, that would allow the gentleman to answer the question. Because if we look at the question, he's being asked now if he knew it was edited. How would he know? I think that -- that he needs to lay a foundation in order to -- for us to understand that the gentleman is competent to answer that question the way it's formed at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm comfortable to answer that question, if I may. I had the privilege of seeing both sets of reports, the UNPROFOR reports and, of course, my own which I sent. I think the term here is "editing" in that it was summarised on both sides, because if you can imagine, as information goes up through the chain, it is -- the most important aspects are pulled out of the daily reports and are then passed up the chain. Not everything is taken verbatim and moved up. But an understanding in some critical situations there was word-for-word placement of reports, and it was not unusual to read a Zagreb report with exactly the same information that I had placed in it. And then, once again, I tried to reiterate that on the UNPROFOR side, I would receive the UNPROFOR report and it was, once again, my words that were in that same report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, on page 17, line 4, they should change something. I didn't say "alterated in any way", just "alterated".

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go down to your reports now since the Defence raised this issue, and I think that we'll give a response in the course of the examination-in-chief. I would like the General to be shown Exhibit 3909. I don't have it on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, please. The registrar tells me this document is under seal. So we have to go into private session if you want to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go into private session, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While that's happening, if I may raise a concern here, and my concern is as follows: The gentleman is being shown some documents, starting with the document that he generated. Obviously he's the most competent person to talk about that. And then from there, he indicated that information would flow up to the CC Travnik and then to RC -- from there, to RC Zenica and then on to Zagreb. My concern is as follows: We saw in the previous document where someone else had injected some information at another level, information that was not contained in his initial report. Although he was competent at least to testify about it, but nonetheless the person who injected that information isn't here to be cross-examined. But more importantly, these documents, especially the executive summary, contain information from other areas, and simply to ask the gentleman whether he was receiving this information and whether he had read this information is insufficient to allow the content of these documents to come in without having someone else to be cross-examined on those areas. He can be cross-examined on Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, and what have you, the areas that he was familiar with, but I fear that at the end they're going to try to introduce all these documents, back-dooring it, by simply saying the gentleman was familiar with it, so obviously everything was true, accurate and complete, and therefore we need not worry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked him a very concise and precise question, the witness, and he responded to this question, and I asked him not to dwell on this issue more at this point because I will ask a specific point on the humanitarian convoys. I am not asking questions relevant to Mostar or other areas. It is already clarified that they received such kind of information. But I'm not going deeper in this document with information not relevant to the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, perhaps my learned friend could answer us: Does he intend to then submit the entire document or only the relevant paragraph to which this gentleman here is familiar? That's the whole issue. So now with that clarification, perhaps he can answer us. Does he expect the entire summary, for instance, the last document, to come in, the executive summary, based on making reference to one particular paragraph, or is it just the one paragraph that he referred the witness to? And if that's the case, fine, I have no objection. But that's the real issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have already made a decision concerning admission of documents, and it's said that if a document was important and consisted of several pages, what will be admitted is the paragraph concerning which questions were asked. So, in response to Mr. Karnavas's objection, in our case it will be paragraph 122, which was already the subject of questions. And I want to ask one. Colonel, concerning paragraph 122 -- are we still in private session? We have to switch back to private session in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: General, some minutes ago you told the Trial Chamber that you had very close cooperation with UNPROFOR company with which you were sharing the office, and you shared information with them. How could you explain that sometimes UNPROFOR, in their documents were references to team -- to ECMM and team V2 as the source of the information?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: If it's a unique situation, which I hope had been duplicated in other places of the region in which we worked, I'm not and I cannot answer, other than the ECLO which was collocated with UNPROFOR headquarters, did the other teams enjoy a closer relationship. Because of the very large area which we covered, and I, as an individual, could only cover so much of that, and once again that Bravo Company had the capability of being in a lot more places than I was, duplicated with the fact that I got to places where they could not, this natural evolution of sharing of information came about. There were times and places where UN, UNPROFOR company commander Graham Binns was attending a meeting in one location and I would be in other location acquiring totally different information or finding out additional. I would arrange meetings as well as UNPROFOR would arrange meetings. And at the end of the day, we'd be able to compare and talk about our experiences and bring them together to try to make a conclusion of what was really happening, since we had access to all areas and levels of military and civilian authorities. I don't think we would ever have gotten a more clearer picture if we had not done it this way. If we would have controlled our own bits of information, we would only have had maybe a half or a quarter of the story. It's because of this comparison and ability to talk to one another that we were able to share information and, consequently, move information up and down both chains of command to allow it to be digested by each of the organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to be shown Exhibit 3822. That is page 3, paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, when they make references to ECMM in the Prozor area, could it be understood that they meant yourself or V2 team as source of the information?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. It is my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now Exhibit 4077.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please turn on his second microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: General, please open page 2, paragraph 10, of this report. I would ask you this same question: Who was the source of this information or this piece of information that's about imam?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Was this information included in your personal report? I mean not personal, I mean team V2 report.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Next, Exhibit 4517.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Page 3, paragraph 11, dealings with the Muslims detained in some detention facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but before we move to this next exhibit, could my learned friend, if he intends to move the previous exhibit into evidence, that is to say, 4077, could it be made clear which part of that document he was showing to the witness, and how much of it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I will explain it very plainly, because some part of my examination-in-chief will be devoted to some specific questions, such as expelling of Muslim -- expulsion of Muslims from Prozor area, detention of Muslims. Now I'm dealing with the system of information, relevance of documents which came from other sources. That was the aim of this part of my examination-in-chief. As for the specific questions on the whole documents, we'll talk about it further when we dwell on specific issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, who was the source of that information?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Are you referring to 4517 now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may put aside this exhibit now. And let's go back to maybe the beginning of our examination-in-chief, because Their Honours already asked some questions and I have to rearrange a little bit my examination-in-chief by just abbreviating it. Witness, what was your understanding of the importance of the Prozor area from the military, economic, and geographic point of view, the strategic point of view of the whole, at the moment when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Because of my background, I think I can make an honest assessment that when I came across Prozor from the south for the very first time, I was somewhat impressed of the dominance of the high ground to the north. And it's only after a period of time spent there did I realise that this piece of ground was very important for that central region and how it was going to be controlled militarily, in that the one that owned that high feature basically dominated all the ground to the south. And realising that lines of communication were somewhat tenuous between Split and into Sarajevo, as well as lines of communication being cut between Mostar and Prozor, you could understand why this piece of ground became more tactically sound to be able to hold onto. Once again, I would suggest that it was more or less driven by terrain rather than an economic base that I could even comment on. It was the fact that this piece of ground was the dominating piece of feature in that middle ground which would allow one side or the other to have control.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now let's go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Before we move to private session, I would like to ask a question concerning the document 4517. On page 1, in paragraph 4, we find the following: "Mario Cerkez, Viteska BDE Commander, claimed to BritBat that Radio Vitez had broadcast an article accusing the ICRC of smuggling ammunition to the Muslims and of moving their snipers." And there is a comment: "The majority of aid agencies are held in low esteem by the HVO in Vitez. However, the ICRC are particularly unpopular in Croat eyes." I would like to ask, Colonel, if you remember any follow-up after this paragraph, I mean after this -- in a way, when this message was received, according to paragraph 4. And do you know any -- about any action that the ICRC might have taken concerning -- to refute the allegations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had connections with ICRC in varying -- at varying times and in varying places. But one of the biggest concerns - and, once again, it was just watching this transition on the ground - was everything in those days was focused, in my opinion I say, on what was happening in Sarajevo. There was not much really understood, myself included until I got into it, about the surrounding areas. Remembering that the "road to salvation," if you want to call it that, which was the road that was going from Split across into Prozor which was maintained by the Brit engineers to sustain Sarajevo and then move up through Gornji Vakuf and then over through Zenica, this whole line of communication was built, if I remember correctly, the winter before. And there were convoys of NGOs, aid workers, humanitarian, UNHCR, UNPROFOR, that were using this road daily. Convoy upon convoy would be coming in. And, of course, Gornji Vakuf and Prozor was one of, you know, the routes that they would travel. And it became very -- I would suggest very disheartening to the locals that saw all this aid going forward into Sarajevo but not really stopping at Prozor or Gornji Vakuf or maybe any other number of places along the way which were just in bad, sort of, situations as others. I can't comment specifically on this paragraph, but I would suggest it's related around those sort of issues of why things became quite sensitive about stuff moving through the area but not really stopping, and to the point where UNHCR convoys would come in ridden with bullets all the way down the convoys, including fuel trucks, and as well as being hijacked on that route and material taken, money taken, and vehicles taken, during my time there. And it was directly related to, I believe, that nothing was stopping here; it was continuing to go north-east into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now I would ask you to turn to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Colonel, you informed the Trial Chamber that you had dealings with local military commanders from both warring factions, both HVO and ABiH. Could you just briefly inform the Trial Chamber who were the commanders in the area of your team from HVO side and ABiH side.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you have touched on the one weakness that I have which is remembering names, and I would have to be referred to documents and confirm that those were the individuals. There are names that stick out for me. Zrinko was in the area of Gornji Vakuf on the HVO side. I think I'm going to stop there because I'm going to need some guidance from the perspective of -- you can show me documents that I have written and I can tell you "Yes, they are" or "No, they were not."

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know -- we are talking about Zrinko. Zrinko, is it his first name?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was his first name, last name, or his pseudonym. I think it was his last name. Yeah. I'd have to look at the documents again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. If you don't remember the names of the commanders, but could you describe the situation in both factions from the point of view of organisation of each military faction, HVO and ABiH. Your impressions, your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I'll predicate my comments by saying that, once again, I was not -- in those days I was not in the information-gathering or intelligence-gathering mode, and I would not have recorded the structures and how they would have been made up because it was not in our mandate. What I can do is give you an opinion what I thought the structure was on the day, and that was, up north was the BiH which were -- ABiH which was controlled out of Bugojno, and the commander of the OZ was in that location in which he had brigades and organisations who were in operations to the south of Prozor and to the south-east, with the realisation that the Serbs were to the north and to the west. To the extreme south of Prozor, they were -- there was also an OZ which was controlled out of Prozor, and its lines stretched from east to west and swung up to the north on the western side, up to the west side of Gornji Vakuf, and was kind of in a semi-horseshoe down to the Makljen checkpoint and then directly to the east. And that was kind of the basic lay of the land that I was able to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have any personal meetings with them?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: On all sides. I did -- at the beginning of -- of this session, we talked about where people were located and, more importantly, who I had contacts with, with the understanding that I had contacts on the ground with individual soldiers; I had contacts with company commanders, battalion commanders, as well as the OZ commander, and right up through the chain in each of the sides. And they were -- the two individuals who I knew were responsible both in -- in Prozor and, of course, north in Bugojno --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What issues --

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: -- which I talked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What issues, what questions, were the subject matter of your discussions with them?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I think it was realising that we were trying to cover everything, and very difficult -- before we -- and in our daily reports, you saw this kind of trend that started to happen, that we would prepare for the next day's activities the night before, and we would try to come up with a series of concerns or questions that we would bring forward to each of the commanders of a particular issue. One example, like I said, is the -- that if we heard of an incident one side, then we would go over and talk to them on the other side. Of course, for security and safety reasons, we did not divulge where that information would ever come from, or who we, in fact, had been talking to. It was a matter of, once again, addressing the humanitarian side of the house as well as gathering general information about the general situation throughout the area and who was doing what to whom. It was a very reactive time which we were involved in, and we were reacting to situations on the ground that were happening. And it was a matter of it being a very active time frame in which things happened, and then we addressed them as we could on the day. There was very little long-range planning for talking or focus on what our work was. It was literally day-to-day management, crisis management, in trying to sort out very difficult situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you address to them questions relevant to the humanitarian situation in the area?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely. Specifically on movement of convoys, movement of humanitarian aid, and movement of individuals. And, in some cases, there was restriction and/or direct assault or attack on these convoys which became very sensitive, and you knew that individuals that were doing this were from the military side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, were from -- what I'm trying to get at is they were somehow linked to the military, and so we would take it to the military commanders as to, do they understand what was happening, did they realise why it was happening, and were there ever attempts to stop it or return stuff or return trucks that had somehow disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you address the issues of war crimes to both commanders?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: The answer is yes. I can remember specifically on a joint meeting that was held, not that I was trying to predict the future, but I can remember openly throwing the Geneva Convention book that I had acquired on a table and getting to my feet and making a very open statement that one day the people around this table would become accountable for their actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have any specific example for that, any specific incident that you addressed to them?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: There was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt, but the question is vague and ambiguous. Addressed to them. To whom? If we're going to get on to such an important subject, can we at least know the individuals with whom the witness was talking?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: The witness -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: The witness does not remember the names of commanders, but he was dealing with commanders of both local factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know what that means. Does it mean in a particular location, Gornji Vakuf? Does it mean commanders at a particular level? Belonging to which side? Even if he doesn't remember the names, can he identify them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Please allow me. You mentioned a meeting between you and the commanders of both factions. It was obviously a meeting that had been organised beforehand. Who had organised it, had you or had they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had organised it. And what I'm referring to as "we" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- is the UNPROFOR commander, Major Binns and myself had organised it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. If you had organised that meeting, you had good reasons for doing so. There must have been an incident. What was the reason? Because if you bring along the Geneva Conventions and you put it on the table and you say to them, "One of these days you will be held accountable for what you have done," there must have been an incident involved. Mr. Murphy would like some clarification on this, and the Bench would also like some clarification. Which incident are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting that I'm referring to specifically had to do with the total deterioration of the situation, and this is around the Bugojno offensive happening by the Muslims in pushing the Croats to the south. And we knew at that point in time that the war was on in that particular area, the battle was on. And we had managed to bring the sides together at the headquarters in the compound at Gornji Vakuf. The meeting I'm referring specifically to, Zrinko was present on behalf of the -- the HVO, and I'm at a loss, once again, for names, but obviously the commander on the -- on the BiH side was also present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This specific situation was dealing with a cease-fire violation that had occurred in the area to the direct west of Gornji Vakuf in which -- remember when I said the HVO had, in fact, occupied on the south side -- sorry, on the west side of Gornji Vakuf and then down to the south. So there was a valley that we could see from our location that they were going at one another. There was a battle going on in the middle of it. And every time we're putting Graham Binns' company in between this, trying to monitor it, and they were constantly being shot at and in the middle of this whole situation. And it was a matter of trying to separate the sides. In the meantime, in those days, there had been all sorts of accusations - and they're in my reports - about atrocities that had occurred from the perspective of finding a mass grave on one side to prisoners of war being used on the front line to dig trenches, and other incidents like this. So this meeting was all around this whole activity. And what I began to realise is that, if the warring factions were going to go at one another, they were going to go at one another, and UNPROFOR nor ECMM could have anything -- or could not prevent it from happening. And it was from that point forward that we moved our efforts not toward the military aspects they were going to play. It was a matter of now moving more toward the humanitarian side and seeing what we could do there. If that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: A very brief question about Prozor military police. Did you have any contacts with military police in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. You're moving on to another topic. We were dealing with an important issue. I shall give you the floor back again. But just to add to what you've just said, from what the Bench understands, you were convinced that an offensive was under way. The offensive was launched by the ABiH and, therefore, the HVO retreated. You then said that some people were found in a mass grave. I don't know who these people were. Were they Croats or Muslims? You didn't mention that. And in the light of all that was happening, you were trying to broker a cease-fire between the two parties. Who were the people in these mass graves? Were they Muslims, Croats, or Serbs? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, this is very much related to the situation which we were talking about earlier about civilians being used as human shields to march them down the battlefield. This particular incident I'm referring to happened in Gornji -- sorry, in Prozor to the -- stop. This incident was dealing specifically with Bugojno, and to the south of Bugojno, we were making our way up one day, just after the HVO had been pushed out, and we came across a gathering of people, a very large crowd of Muslims. The first thing they did was jump in front of my vehicle and claim that there has been a mass grave found of which their soldiers or individuals had been killed and dumped. Being in a situation where I was -- I was in the process of trying to find out what was happening, I also made the comment that we had to be careful about calling this a war crime. And I remember walking over to the site of which bodies were being pulled out. But what caught my eye was that the bodies all contained uniforms. And it was my quick estimation on the day that, in fact, it was not a mass gave but, in fact, of soldiers of that had been buried. Once again, we would have to go back into my reports and specifically to how I reported it, but I can remember, you know, saying that I cannot make an opinion that, in fact, it was a mass killing or a mass grave or anything. The individuals in the grave had been shot. There was no evidence other than they had been shot. And, once again, I had reported it into our documents, and it was well beyond my purview to make any sort of comment or judgement on that activity, other than that there were lots of bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were wearing an ABiH uniform, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four, that I can remember, in that site. And what was -- I just want to bring this around to see how out of control things can get. After we had done this walkabout and taken as much information as we could and sent it up higher, and my comment was that, "I can't tell you what this is; we need the experts down here." I wrote that in my report. And the very next day I drive up there and, of course, I run into more residents who claim that the -- the ECMM has declared this a killing -- or, sorry, a mass grave and war crimes. And I said, "Wait a minute. I'm the guy. I was guy who was here yesterday and I'm telling you I cannot make that opinion." So it's amazing how things kind of just flowed one into the other, and a situation that probably could get out of control very quickly as to whether it was or was not. And to this day, I cannot tell you whether, in fact, it was just soldiers that were buried because of deterioration of bodies or the fact that it was, in fact, an execution of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may try to save us some time. For the past two and a half or maybe three pages, we have been discussing almost exclusively Gornji Vakuf in 1993, at the time when the witness was there, May 1993, and there was reference to Bugojno. That's the latter part. Let us remind ourselves that Gornji Vakuf is mentioned in the indictment only for the period of January 1993, and Bugojno is totally absent from the indictment. So the Prosecution is now examining the witness on irrelevant things. I do not really understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I respectfully disagree with Mr. Kovacic. I didn't ask any question about Gornji Vakuf in 1993, in June or July. I did not ask any questions relevant to Bugojno. I was questioning the witness about Prozor. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed with the questions on Prozor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My question was about military police in Prozor. Did you have any contacts with the military police in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on many different occasions. Because of where they were located, their building, which was right at the U-junction at the bottom of the hill, we would pass by this location every couple of days and we got to know these -- we had contact with these individuals from that point on. I always tended to make a point of stopping in and trying to find out information from them, and basically get a feel of what was happening in Prozor. I also met the military police in a variety of different locations, a variety of different individuals, on the route all the way up to the Makljen checkpoint and to areas surrounding Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the chief of the military police in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of his deputy?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do not. Other than if I had recorded it in my daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And my question is now: Did you have an impression that the military police was properly carrying out its functions on maintaining law and order in the area?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Going back to what I believe -- or what we referred to them as paramilitary, were they carrying out their functions? I would say definitely yes, but the method in which they carried them out was what I have -- is what I would question. I would suggest that they used a form of -- I'll use -- for lack of a better term right now, but a form of terrorist tactics in order to keep the population under control or within the realm. They had freedom of movement, and you could tell that -- if I was in a situation where I was talking to the locals or a particular side - I'm referring to if I was talking to the Muslim women and children - these individuals would be around me. There would be very distinctive eye contact between the person I was talking to and those individuals that were, I believe, military police, and the avoidance of that eye contact, or would, in fact, try to avoid to say anything that would -- might be used against them at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Colonel, while there is silence, could you describe more precisely what you refer to by speaking of terrorism tactics? Can you refer to more specific forms of behaviour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I -- that's why I said I have to be careful in using that term. I mean, there is no doubt in my mind who ran the town, if you get that sort of image, and I referred to them earlier as, you know, the sheriff and his posse. You know, they had the freedom of movement. They restricted people they didn't want to move. There was always this fearful sort of feeling I got every time I went into the town, especially those of the Muslims. I talk specifically about the wives and the children -- or the women and the children that were in that particular area that were restricted to move anywhere. I had personal conversations with more than one female that had indicated that they were being selected and taken out from the camp in the night, during the night, and these individuals were doing sexual acts, including rape, and then returning the women back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This lady who told you that, did you immediately go to the superior authority on the military side in Prozor to tell him about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a lady, it was ladies. If I remember, there were at least two. I would have no doubt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's even more reason to go and see somebody about it. Did you bring up this problem? Did you draw the attention of the authorities to that? Because you were a representative of the European Mission. You represented the European Mission on the ground, so you were somebody important. So what did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, there is no doubt what I would do, because I'm an individual that tends to deal with the issue right on the spot. If I would have found out something like that, which I did, I would have taken it immediately to the military police commander and to the area commander, the Operational Zone commander, and I would have told him that. I can tell you that categorically. It's my personality to do that. And I can remember specifically on those days talking to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly what I'm getting to, sir, is that on that day, I can remember taking it to the guard commander in charge of this small containment of women and children, and the initial response was, "Us? No, we would never do something like that. And more importantly, we're here to protect these people. We are protecting the front and the back end." But what was happening was that these individuals were coming in from the east and the west, across the ground which there were no roads and then dragging individuals out. Once again, other than the hearsay of the ladies that told me that and me confronting the individuals on the spot and then eventually taking that to the military police commander and then following on to the Operational Zone commander, that was all that I could do within that time frame, realising the -- you know, how big a problem we were involved in. Remember, we were right in the middle of a battle. And this was only one of many different problems that were happening in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You say that it was a small problem in a sea of problems, but this minor problem was the reason, among others, why this Tribunal was instituted and why we are here. The commander of this Operational Zone, first of all, who was he? And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you remind me of the name, I would say absolutely. His last name started with an S. I just -- as I said, my mind's gone blank right at the present time as to his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never mind the name for the moment. What did he tell you when you said to him, "I just talked to women who explained to me that several of them had been taken out by night by individuals and raped"? What did he say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm honestly trying to search for that time and that frame about that specific event, and I would only be placing words in somebody's mouth that may not have been said about that specific event. I honestly do remember taking it to that individual and telling him about it. Now, as I've said, there were a lot of things happening, and you've already addressed the fact that this is one of the important reasons why we're here today, but other than probably trying to, once again, refer back to my daily report from 13 years ago would I be able to give you an answer specifically of what he did say or did not say. But there is no doubt in my mind that I did bring this information to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, is the big issue of freedom of movement of humanitarian convoys. What was the situation in your area of responsibility as from May through August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I think from the humanitarian -- first of all, to understand the humanitarian convoys, there were many and from a multitude of organisations that moved up and down freely on that road. Initially when I arrived, the freedom of movement was totally unrestricted, and everybody - I'll refer to this as a mom-and-pop shop - that have one or two vehicles and have the desire to go help people, of one or two trucks to move it, was able to use it all the way up to the larger humanitarian organisations, like the UNHCR, were able to travel up and down the road. And we would see all types. As the situation started to deteriorate, so did the threat directly against those convoys moving on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, one question. When did the situation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: One question. When did the situation start deteriorating?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: To be quite honest, you know, I arrived -- within a week of me arriving in Gornji Vakuf. You know, we're looking at the end of May. And as I said, there were incidents already starting -- there were indicators that things were starting to happen. But it really got rotten the end of July and the end of August. But, you know, as time went on, it just got more and more restrictive, and eventually it was a situation of UNPROFOR, and specifically Graham Binns' company, literally being ordered to take on convoy escort duty of UN convoys because we did not have the resources to escort non-UN convoys, and non-UN convoys were ambushed along the way. And UN convoys, even though they were under the escort of UNPROFOR, were, in fact, shot up, targeted and were, once again, riddled with bullets as they arrived in our location in Gornji Vakuf. The convoy -- the UNPROFOR -- sorry, the UNHCR convoys that were not escorted were, in one case I know specifically, hijacked and vehicles were stolen and people were robbed, et cetera, et cetera. So as time went on, all the way into August, it just got -- the number of NGOs and non -- of humanitarian organisations were drastically reduced because of danger on the route, and definitely there was danger in my area, which is that when it entered into Prozor up into Gornji Vakuf and then from Gornji Vakuf over towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the most notorious incidents with humanitarian convoys in your area of responsibility that were reported by you to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: The one that stands out in my mind became known as the Tuzla 500. The Tuzla 500 convoy was made up of about, if I remember correctly, 512 trucks that had gone out from Tuzla the month before and had gathered supplies from the area of Split, including taking on more vehicles --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what month? What month was it?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: End of June, if I'm not mistaken. It's recorded, once again, in my reports, when we took on responsibility for that convoy. I think it was June or July. Once again, I'd have to refer specifically to date and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You have the opportunity of seeing your reports, but now I would like to hear just your information.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I think it fell apart. Okay. The Tuzla 500, a story in itself. It all started with this 500 -- we got word through the chain, through our Capsat, that there was a convoy made up of the locals of Tuzla who had taken upon themselves to -- because the area of Tuzla was surrounded and were running out of supplies, they took it upon themselves to run trucks out to Split to gather as much as they could, including fuel, food, clothing, whatever. And by the time this thing started to move, like I said, it was 500-plus vehicles. On the move, it was 14.2 kilometres long; when it was stopped, it was about 5.1 kilometres in length, when all trucks were parked behind one another. The Tuzla 500 arrived. And we got word that it was coming, then wasn't coming; coming, then wasn't coming. Up through our chain we were trying to determine where and what our responsibilities were for this convoy. I had concern because, hearing the number of vehicles, I knew darn well that 500 vehicles, with all the drivers and some co-drivers and some with even families, could not be protected by a company worth of people. It is impossible. The response that basically had come back, "It is not a UN convoy; it is not our responsibility." There was -- I still had concern because I knew that we were going to naturally inherit this convoy. It was coming to our area and we had no choice but to take it on. We knew something was -- and, like I said, we could already start feeling things were starting to deteriorate in the area. My partner and I kept UNPROFOR informed about this convoy, what we knew about it and when it was coming. And we went to the area to the west of Prozor in order to meet up with the convoy. We sat there for about 24 hours and still no sign of the convoy. We went back to Gornji Vakuf and we got word once again that it was on its way, and they expected the trucks to arrive the next day, and I want to say early in the morning, probably about 9.00 or 10.00. My partner and I, with our driver, proceeded down to Prozor. Just as we were arriving in Prozor, the front end of the convoy arrives. At the bottom of the hill in Prozor, there is a Y-intersection. The one road to the south goes to Mostar; the other road to the north heads up the switchbacks up to the Makljen checkpoint. These trucks were arriving en masse, one behind the other. What was strange when I came around the corner was to find the military police of the building at the bottom of the hill actually doing traffic control. I was somewhat stunned that they knew how to do it. And I jumped out of my vehicle and I quickly noticed that for every four or five vehicles that was being pushed up the road to the Makljen checkpoint, there was another vehicle -- one of the vehicles of the convoy were being hived off or being separated from the convoy and being pushed down the road, down toward the Mostar road. I quickly -- I'm adding things up here, and it makes sense that at this stage and point in time, the vehicles are being systematically separated from one another. Once again, I had no understanding why they had even business in doing this, and I relate back to my original comment: Here was humanitarian aid that, once again, was going through the Prozor area of which nothing was there for Prozor. And it was then that I made a quick decision to confront the individuals on the checkpoint to tell them, what are they doing; this is not their convoy. It's not a UN convoy or anything. At that particular time I was forced to leave at gunpoint, being told it was none of my business.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: By whom? By whom?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: By the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know that person before?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I knew that person from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: He was a deputy military police commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: In Prozor or --

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: In Prozor. Never having to be told twice, I moved away from the situation which I monitored from about 200 metres away. And because of the Brit radio, I had to move anyways because the Brit radio only -- because the low ground, and realising where the Brits were in Gornji Vakuf, on high ground, I could not communicate at that intersection with them. I went 200 metres down the road, immediately got communication, and I called the Brit company, informed Graham Binns that we had a situation ongoing at the base of the hill. And I said, "You've got to get a platoon down here with Warrior in order to sort it out." And I said I would remain in location but "I can't do a darn thing right at the present time." Upon that, Graham also realised how grave the situation was going to become and that we, once again, were inheriting this humanitarian convoy which was none of our business. And within a matter of 15 to 20 minutes, I had a platoon of Warrior down there, of which the platoon commander I ordered to place his vehicles to block the road down to Mostar. So they were -- they were forced to continue on their way up the Makljen checkpoint. The military police, realising they were out-gunned, backed away. We managed to get the rest of the vehicles going, and, unfortunately, at the top of the hill was the Makljen checkpoint which was controlled by the HVO. At that stage, the Makljen checkpoint was closed on us. We could not push forward the convoy, and it was a good thing that we didn't, because what had transpired in the area of Travnik, while this convoy had been in Split, was an all-out battle to the north of us, which would have run this convoy into a very unfavourable position. So stopping it at the Makljen checkpoint allowed us to actually start to protect, inherit to protect the convoy. And what I mean by that is, we were able to take the convoy and run it all the way back and forth across switchbacks all the way from the Makljen checkpoint, all the way down to Prozor. So these vehicles were able to be kept up against the side of the mountain. One, access was denied from those trying to get in; two, we were able to control who got in and out; and, more importantly, three, that if we had incorrect fire, i.e., military -- sorry, artillery or mortar fire, that the convoy could not be reached. They were safe. And, once again, these were drivers and co-drivers and family members that were in this convoy. At the back of the convoy were fuel trucks. The thing I would bring to the attention of this Tribunal is that a full tanker full of fuel and the cost of that fuel I could only imagine is probably, in those days, well over $100.000 for a tanker full of fuel. In the meantime, we are consistently being told that we are not responsible for this convoy. Somehow, we thought we had become because they were in our area. And over a period of week, we -- they sat in our area waiting for the battle to end in the north. But in the meantime we were trying to keep things safe. For that evening we parked the vehicles all along, all the way up. With the limited resources, realising there were other things to do in our area of responsibility - Graham had other things to do with his company than protect this - we managed to put one vehicle at the front of the convoy at the Makljen checkpoint and a second vehicle at the back of the convoy. That whole convoy length, I repeat, was 5.2 kilometres long from front to back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Earlier on, Colonel, you had spoken about 14 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the move, the convoy was 14.2 kilometres, because vehicles would travel about 200 metres between each other. When they're bumper to bumper, they're 5.2 kilometres. If you ask me how I know that, in my real job, I am a recce guy, and we actually drove this convoy many, many times and we actually took mileage and I recorded it as such because I couldn't believe it. You know, of course, my military mind is saying, How do you protect something this big? And what do you do about it? Up against the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
