utterances.text: I'm sorry. In the record we have one figure which is 5.2 kilometres and the next one is 4.2, but I recall you saying 5.2. Line 24 as compared to line 18.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again it's probably my fast English. 14.2 kilometres long on the move and 5.2 kilometres stationary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we're at the Makljen checkpoint with the convoy 5.2 kilometres long, with a Warrior parked at the front end and a Warrior parked at the back end. And that evening everything has calmed down. We got back the vehicles that had somehow gone down the Mostar road, and we thought life was good. I went back to Gornji Vakuf. The next morning I come back and I start to hear that, in the middle of the night, trucks had been removed from the convoy by force and taken back down to Prozor and emptied. And I'm referring to the fuel trucks at the back. I never did ascertain whether it was one, two, or any more than that. But there were fuel trucks that were moved off. And doing further investigation, I found out that this had been done by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: By whom, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: By the military police that were from Prozor. As time progressed, once again, in consultation with Graham Binns, I ascertained that we've got to move this convoy because now it's being threatened from the very town they just moved through, to the point where, in fact, drivers were being taken out from their vehicles and actually beaten. I moved -- I managed to bring this to the attention of the Operational Zone commander, telling him, "What's going on here?" And he says, "I know nothing about this," and he was trying to separate, and he says, "It's not our convoy. We have nothing to do with this. We just want to get it out of our area." And I said, "Well, fine. Then open up the Makljen checkpoint and we can push it on through." In the meantime, I had worked it out and talked with the ABiH commander that if the convoy was in their area they would protect it, and I said that was a lot better than what we had at the Makljen. So in the process, we got the Makljen checkpoint opened, and we moved the convoy to the south of Gornji Vakuf. It was still 5.2 kilometres long. The next night became a very interesting night, because, once again, Graham only had the resources to put a protection on the front and the back of it; but now I was getting reports up and down the line, and I spent the night there in the middle of the convoy, that military forces were coming out from the woods on either side of the convoy and attacking drivers. And the drivers of the convoy started to congregate together or come together in order to start to protect themselves. It was at that point that I couldn't quite figure out who was doing what to whom, and I -- I saw a car coming down the middle of the road. I jumped out in the middle of the road and I stopped, and out jumps our friendly military policeman from Prozor. I confront them. I say, "What are you guys doing here?" and, through my translator, was told, "They're here to protect the convoy." I said, Well, do you realise that they are people, or soldiers coming from the woods on either side that are actually attacking the convoy?" They said,"Oh, yeah, we know that. That's why we're here." In my naivete of the situation, I backed away, they took off, and then I realised they were the ones that were actually doing and actually confronting the drivers. And because the Warriors were at the front and the back end, they were unable to steal trucks directly, because the order had been given to Graham to stop any vehicle from leaving that 5.2-kilometre stretch. But these guys were jumping in and out of the convoy all the way along, coming at them from all different directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, one second. While talking about Graham, do you mean Graham Binns?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, Graham Binns is who I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may ask a question. You said that you realised that the attackers were members of the military police, those who came from the woods.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And how did you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the guys I had seen before. This was the same gang that was in these vehicles, that move around in civilian vehicles, and I recognised the guys as soon as I saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would that be the same guys we refer to as Kinder platoon? I mean, you then described the group which might be the same, although you explicitly denied having known that name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I said that's the first time I'd ever heard that name used for them. But they were all young guys. Whether -- and I would suggest 18 to 22. You know, they were young guys. And if that's the term that was being used, then I would have to say yes, that's the same group. But it was the same group that I had been dealing with, you know, for the full time that I had been there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, did you have any meetings with military authorities afterwards?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, on both sides. One from the HVO to say what was happening, and they said, "Well, it isn't our people who are doing this." And then on the armija side, to say, "I want to move this convoy into your area. Are you going to be able to ensure security?" And eventually I had secured that. So what I, in fact, did was stack the convoy. And what I mean by that is, on the road I put them side by side by side. So instead of being 5.2, it shrunk it right down real quick. Because from Gornji Vakuf was the front vehicle; 5.2 kilometres back was almost at the Makljen checkpoint -- well, in that direction. And then by stacking it by, you know, three lanes and pushing it all up, it got out of the area of responsibility of the HVO and was now all in the area of the BiH. And was able -- at that point in time, I was able to have Graham secure the back and front end. We could actually see the front and the back from sitting in the middle. And from that point on, the convoy was relatively secure in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have any meeting with the chief or commander of the operation zone specifically on this issue together with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I don't know if I did it with UNPROFOR, but I can definitely state I had it. I did. I mean, because it all started to add up as to what had happened over the last two days, before I managed to push everything forward, that, you know, certain selected trucks were being targeted - and I refer directly to the fuel trucks - as well as the second night where drivers were actually being attacked. Now, remember in this convoy, the Tuzla 500, as I understood, it was a mixture of the ethnic background of all three sides, and there were men, women, and children in this convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to be shown Exhibit 2709.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. We have to have a break now. I would like the registrar to calculate how much time the Prosecutor has had, and you still have an hour left. It will be 6.00 when we resume. It would be ideal if you could finish your examination-in-chief over the next hour. The witness should still be here tomorrow. So we shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. According to our calculations, the Prosecution has had 1 hour and 34 minutes, so we have an hour left. So please do your best, and otherwise you will have 30 minutes left tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will do my best, but I'm afraid I will not cover all the questions I planned to cover for this examination-in-chief. So I would like witness to be shown Exhibit 2709, and that will be page 4 in hard copy, paragraph 7. It begins with the words "Following hijacking ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please read it out. Witness, did you participate in this meeting that they're talking about in the report?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I honestly do not recall. Once again, I would have to refer to my daily report. This could have easily been one of these incidents where I was somewhere else and Graham Binns, as the OC, was actually the one that took that, realising the words that stand out are "hostile," and the fact that I may have been sitting with the convoy while he went down, trying to sort out of the situation and retrieve the fuel trucks. So my only statement: I could have or could not have been. I do not remember being in a meeting with those amount of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. And my last question relevant to humanitarian convoys: You said that a deputy of the military police of Prozor was the one who was involved in the incident at the checkpoint. Did you see him afterwards?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did he retain his position in the military police?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have any other information about persons being punished for their involvement in hijacking of military convoys and looting?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I was to understand that no such act took place. Business was as usual in the military structure. The same people were in location doing their business. So I have no idea whether they were or were not punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My next set of questions now. Witness, at some point you were away from the area and came back on the 23rd of July, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct. I went home on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you notice any changes in the situation in the area of your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely. This is where the situation up north in Bugojno had completely deteriorated. HVO had been moved south, and there were two -- there was a distinct line between north and south.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: General, Your Honour just proposed me to abbreviate a little bit my examination-in-chief, so we will be limiting ourselves now to humanitarian issues, the humanitarian situation in your area of responsibility in the course of your mission. So, at the beginning of the examination-in-chief, you said that you dealt with the civilian authorities in Prozor area. Did you have meetings with the mayor of the municipality or the town of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have an impression that he was well aware of the situation in the area?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Within his area of responsibility. What I'm referring to is that he knew what was happening in his town; however, the movement of people, the military actions in and around the town, he had no responsibility or even full knowledge of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to be shown Exhibit 9627. It's not under seal, so we can discuss it in the open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You had asked me at the beginning the name of my partner. It's on the back of this report. And it's Gerritsen, Rudy Gerritsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It came to mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. I would like you to take a look at paragraph 2 of the document. Was it you who had a meeting with the mayor of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were talking about issues relevant to the situation with the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Not just the Muslim population, the population in general, of which was indicated that about 30 per cent, as per my report, were still -- were still there. You can see the breakdown of numbers. So it just wasn't dealing with Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. But out of an abundance of caution, would my learned friend like to check whether this document really is not under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: No, it's not under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So they were talking about approximately 4.600 people moved out of the area?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: How did he explain this situation?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I can only assume that he was having a great deal of difficulty housing everybody, and even though Muslims were being moved from the town of Prozor, he was substantiating the movement by saying, "Well, we've got to move them because there's just too many people in the town." That's what I'm assuming he was trying to get across here. And that it was being overpopulated by displaced persons. Because, once again, I think the mayor only had a piece of the puzzle as to actually what was happening. And, of course, he's saying, "I can't support everybody here. I can't give everybody what they require. And maybe it's not all bad that we move people out in order to care for the people that are remaining."

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You also told the Trial Chamber that you were dealing with representatives of religious professions. Did you have dealings with anyone from the Prozor Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I regularly tried to and had visited the imam who had remained in Prozor throughout the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Was it the same person throughout your period?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, once again, I would have to refer directly to a document with his name on it, and I think one of these documents does have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Sorry. If I may refer to the bottom of that document we were just talking about, again, there is an example where I had been restricted to see the imam.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: That's my next question. Okay. You claim now that you had some restrictions. What kind of restrictions did you have?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: In every attempt -- realising that the imam's house was less than two blocks away from the military police compound or the military police house, I should say, at the corner, every time we made -- attempted to drive up, we were quickly surrounded or told that we could not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Told by whom?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: By the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But did you address the situation to the military authorities or to operation zone authorities?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I would say yes because they're in the same town. And in my -- in my conversation, once again, I've got to reflect back to all the other -- if something on the day happened like that, there would be no doubt I would actually go and be talking to the Operational Zone commander and say, "What has been going on here?" or "What's the reason for it?"

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 9620. That's page 1, paragraph 2, "Political Situation."

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You were the one who drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And is it correct, your allegation, that the Muslims were sent out to come area inhabited by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: What I recall is that I was being told they were being relocated south into other towns. Somewhere in one of my reports I probably can even -- I probably already mention what those towns were. The area which was -- or the interesting point was, once again, we came upon this situation by driving down the road, and as we -- that morning, which is probably the 30th of August, while coming down from the Makljen checkpoint, I was -- and I had discovered -- we had discovered this containment of Muslim women and children to the east side of the road that I -- I made it a point that I was going to check in on them on a regular basis. So on that particular day, in moving down the road, it was at that point in time I caught the last truck turning out of that contained area onto the major road heading for Mostar. It was -- or down toward the Mostar area. In confrontation and conversation with the people on the ground, they told me that everybody had been taken from there. Now, what I'm reading between the lines is, right after that I, of course, went and he saw the mayor and said, "What has happened to these people?" And that's why I made the comment before this that the mayor really, really didn't know the whole situation and only knew a piece of the puzzle. He wasn't aware that they were going to be moved, where they were going to be moved, or what they were up to. There was no doubt in my mind that this was a military operation that moved these people. It had nothing to do with civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: That's page 5 in the hard copy. Electronic version, page 7. Exhibit number 02817. It begins: "V2 attended a joint patrol."

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did your team participate in that mission?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what did you discover there?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: In travelling down that road, all I -- one of the vivid memories that stands out is that houses were put on fire, and there was actual individuals moving from house to house to actually burn the houses. And then by working our way further to the east, we went up into these two small villages that are indicated in the area of Rat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now we should go back to a private session, because we'll have a number of documents which are under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Exhibit number 9619. It's a short document. Was it drafted by you?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What about the number of Muslims living there at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Once again, I'll put this on the table, that we were one team. It was impossible for us to count every single individual that was in that town. This is probably just a general feeling of what was going on. And, if you note, this was the day that we, you know, just basically started asking questions around the area as to what was happening, and, more importantly, what was happening with the Muslim population, specifically with Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now Exhibit 9621. That's the paragraph "Humanitarian Activity," paragraph 4. And this document was drafted on the 20th of August.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And the previous documents were just drafted on the 10th of August and close dates. And now we see in these documents the same information, that you were prevented from visiting some areas. Was it correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And how would you explain the decision to prohibit you visiting those areas? What was the foundation for that, if any?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I can only offer an opinion here that they didn't want us to know what was really happening in each of those areas, either, as I already stated there, what I think was happening, which was the rape and the assaults; and number two, that they had intent, probably, to move people elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Exhibit 9627. Again, paragraph 4, "Humanitarian Activity."

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: That's about the conditions of life.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Is it correct that conditions of life were horrible?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes. For the Muslim community, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And they say about Muslim men, the age from 16 to 60 years, being arrested.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct, because in each of the community -- or every time we visited the -- what stood out in my mind, every time we visited groups of Muslims, it was children and women. The men were not there. And children, I'm saying up to probably the age of 16 or 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Next exhibit, 9630. That's about -- my question is: Were the Muslim people in the areas allowed to leave? Did they have an opportunity of moving around freely?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: In my opinion, they did not have the freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Why do you think so?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Well, I go back to the one place that really stands out, which is that area to the east of the main road up to the Makljen checkpoint, and which there were guards on the roadways in and out of this location. And the houses were occupied by women and children in very large amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you at some point see Muslim detainees in the area?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And if you're referring to men, yes. I had been taken to -- and this is all related around the fact of communicating with both sides and trying to ascertain about prisoners of war or those that were detained. And it is through many discussions that finally it was revealed that there was a location where Muslim men had been taken. And I believe that number was around 160 to 170 men had been retained or detained at a technical school on the side of the hill in Prozor, which eventually I got access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You're saying "eventually".

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please expand a little bit on that. Who prevented you from visiting detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Well, first off is the -- is trying to determine whether it even existed. Secondly, once we realised that one existed, it was then getting access to it, and the admittance that there was such place in Prozor. And, I mean, I could only have gotten that information from the Operational Zone commander. One day, finally, he says, "Yes, we do have it." And then me pushing on the fact that these men were being detained and that I would want -- I want to go visit them. And the other thing that stood out prior to this - and maybe it was an issue of, you know, too much evidence was there - was I can remember moving between Gornji Vakuf and Prozor and watching soldiers working in the fields to the left and right of the main road running north/south. So they're on the east and the west side of the road and they were digging trenches. But what was interesting was there were soldiers standing around with weapons. And that didn't exactly add up as to why there need to be -- if they're digging trenches, why there needed to be soldiers with weapons actually in the carrying position. And I started -- in my mind, started to put things together and said, "Wait a minute. The people doing the digging of the ditches or the trenches aren't necessarily those soldiers of --" yeah, back up. I would suggest that they were being guarded to carry on an activity, which was digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But were they soldiers? Were they dressed in the kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Once again, uniform -- how do you describe a uniform? If you say that some were dressed in camouflage-pattern pants or tops, then the answer is yes; and if you call that a uniform, then yes. It was a mixture of everything and anything. Some were in running shoes; some were in combat boots. And, like I said, a variety of different dress on the top. But, I mean, they were in a quasi-military uniform, I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And were the soldiers who were guarding them dressed in a kind of uniform as well?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were dressed in a more formal uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Which uniform? What military faction?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Realising that I'm watching this from afar, I would suggest that it was HVO because it was HVO territory to the south of Bugojno -- or sorry, south of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now I would ask Trial Chamber to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 04517.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: That's paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: They are making reference to information that they had got from ECMM.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes. And that information would have come from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And here you're talking about the people digging trenches. Do you mean the same situation you just told us today?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing that I would draw your attention to is the dates. This is a report from the 26th, and my original report which actually spoke of this on the 19th and the 20th, which eventually got pushed up, this may have been another -- another specific incident which I would have picked up on driving from Gornji Vakuf down into Prozor, or vice versa; that I, once again, saw another group of men in the sidelines of the road actually doing digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just finished this part of my questioning, but I also have some questions relevant to Mr. Praljak and a couple of other issues. But, of course, perhaps it makes no sense to start doing it now. It will not take me too long, I mean my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time or how many minutes will you need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, I will cope with it in 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said you had questions to Mr. Praljak and a number of other issues. Couldn't you address the other issues now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, maybe one issue I can address now. Now we're in open session so we can speak freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Colonel, did you ever get information about cooperation of the Serbian army in the area with one of the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please expand a little bit on that. What faction?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: At the point in time where I had, or I was about to -- it's either just before I went on leave or just after I went on leave, we managed -- I indicated beforehand the situation where the warring factions had turned against one another in the Bugojno area. And as a result of that, you ended up with BiH being in the north and in the south, and with about, if I remember the figure correctly, some 15.000 mixture of military and civilians that were pinned between the two sides, between Bugojno in the north and Gornji Vakuf in the south, and remembering that the Serbs were occupying the area to the north of Bugojno and to the west of Bugojno. So there was this kind of squeeze that had happened, with a small pocket of 15.000 Croats which were surrounded on the north, east, and south, and the Serbs were on the west. We went in there, and we managed -- into this pocket, and during that time, we managed to pull out at least two busloads, if I remember correctly, of injured while under fire. Certain things were happening. We managed to extract these people. We knew it was difficult. The next day, we went back and this whole area that had contained this 15.000-plus people had disappeared, had gone. We deduced that there was only one place they could have gone and that was into Serb territory. And it was through further investigation and eventually going south down to Prozor did we find out exactly what happened. And that group of individuals that had been pinned from the north, east, and west had, in fact, brokered a passage through Serb territory to the west and then south back into Prozor. So Prozor took a large influx of individuals into the area from -- the people from up north in Bugojno, which probably included the commander and his soldiers from that area. So there was a small town to the north-west of Prozor which I know had been occupied by a majority of these people, and as well the civilians were now being shuttled back from that location out of the area, out of the zone, out of the combat zone, and with a view that they were being pushed down toward the Tomislavgrad area, if I can remember correctly. So that's what I know about the crossing of lines into Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I think that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now 7.00. I would like to invite all and everyone to return tomorrow morning when the hearing shall resume. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomorrow.
